Title: Another democratic socialist victory – Angie Nixon in Florida – sends shock waves through party establishment
Content: It wasn’t supposed to be this way. In conservative Florida, Alex Vindman – a retired army intelligence officer who blew this whistle on Donald Trump in his first term – appeared set to carry the Democratic establishment banner as the party staged a long-shot bid to topple a Republican US senator. Florida’s Democratic voters had other ideas. Democratic socialist Angie Nixon emerged a surprise victor in the US Senate primary on Tuesday, after a campaign in which she was outfunded and outspent by Vindman at a ratio of more than 10 to one. Her triumph sent shock waves through the Democratic party machine as it prepares to mount a challenge to the incumbent Republican senator, Ashley Moody, in November’s US midterm elections. Nixon, a tenacious leftwing fighter and former union organizer who has represented Jacksonville in the Florida house since 2020, raised $975,000 in her campaign, as against Vindman’s $16.3m, but garnered more than 750,000 votes to her opponent’s 550,000 – an overwhelming victory that left his campaign scratching its head as to where it all went wrong. “The reason that we all collectively thought that he was the favorite was because he had that national name recognition, and especially because he was able to raise so much money,” said Aubrey Jewett, professor of political science at the University of Central Florida. She noted, however, that polling largely focused on how Nixon and Vindman would respectively fare against Moody in a general election, rather than whether Democratic voters preferred Nixon or Vindman as their party’s candidate. “Is Florida ready for a democratic socialist candidate in a general election? I still don’t know the answer,” added Jewett. “But what this primary showed was that, within the Democratic party base, there is a strong majority of progressive social Democrats in Florida – just like there apparently is across the country.” Nixon’s victory followed a series of primary wins for progressive candidates this summer, including in Philadelphia, Colorado, Michigan and New York City. She only recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America, and was not endorsed by them. She is also set to face trial next month – charged with trespassing and resisting an officer without violence – after a sit-in protest at the office of the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, in May. It remains to be seen how attractive Nixon will be to Florida’s wider electorate in November. As Jewett notes, Florida is heavily populated by Hispanic communities, and Moody is certain to try to affix the “socialist” label to Nixon’s campaign that has long proven toxic at the ballot box for such voter groups. The conservative commentator Noah Rothman, writing in National Review on Wednesday, went one step further, characterizing Nixon as “communist-curious”. “Even if the race for Senate in Florida is now a foregone conclusion, this race will still feature prominently in the national conversation,” he argued. “Why? Because it demonstrates that Republicans are right when they warn that the socialist phenomenon is coming to a town near you.” Pollsters already appear to have concluded that Nixon’s primary victory has limited Democrats’ chances of taking the seat. Within hours of her fiery victory speech on Tuesday night, Sabato’s Crystal Ball, the respected analytical wing of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, moved the Florida Senate race from “likely Republican” to “safe Republican”. It also leaves Democratic leaders in the US Senate, who publicly warmly welcomed Nixon’s win, in something of a quandary. While their path to reclaiming control of the upper chamber from Republicans was never predicated on success in Florida, Vindman, as a moderate, was considered to have at least an outside shot of an upset. Accordingly, the party’s hierarchy was preparing to send dollars and resources to bolster his campaign. Now, with Nixon on the ticket, analysts expect a rethink. “The Democratic establishment was more comfortable with Vindman,” Jewett said. “He had a demonstrated track record of being able to raise money, and Nixon does not.” Florida has about 1.5 million more registered Republican voters than Democrats, she noted. “Nixon is really going to have her work cut out for her to show that she can raise money, or if she can’t, to show that somehow they can recreate the success of the grassroots campaign that brought her victory here,” Jewett added. Her supporters are certain that will be possible. Among a flood of tributes to her on Tuesday night and through Wednesday were calls for unity, including from Vindman himself, who said: “I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me.” Some of the messages were also critical of Vindman, and those in Democratic circles who bet on the wrong horse. “Angie Nixon’s win sent shock waves through the Democratic establishment who got too comfortable behind corporate donors and moderate candidates,” said Hayley Margolis, an organizer with Jewish Voice for Peace South Florida. “Her votes were hard earned through heartfelt grassroots conversations with the working class across the state of Florida.” Nixon, who was reprimanded for using a bullhorn on the Florida house floor earlier this year, does not care for internal party wrangling. And she made one thing clear: she is unlikely to change tack as she presents herself to the wider statewide electorate before November. “They look at this movement and they call us extreme, they call us radical, but I think people see through that. I won’t let them define me and I know you will always know where I stand,” she told supporters on Tuesday night. “If believing a mom shouldn’t have to work three jobs to keep a roof over her head is extreme, call me extreme. Ashley Moody can call me whatever she wants, but in November she’ll be calling me senator.”

Title: Can Andy Burnham rewire the ‘Treasury brain’ to boost growth?
Content: Andy Burnham is far from the first prime minister to dream of taming the power of the mighty Treasury. Boris Johnson all but forced the resignation of Sajid Javid by handpicking his team; Margaret Thatcher favoured her economic adviser Alan Walters over Nigel Lawson, prompting the latter’s furious resignation; and Tony Blair and Gordon Brown’s power struggle was the stuff of Whitehall legend. Burnham’s approach harks further back still to Labour prime minister Harold Wilson’s Department for Economic Affairs (DEA), a short-lived attempt to bring long-term thinking to British economic policymaking. The PM made the historical analogy as he gave fresh details this week of his plan to take control of growth policy from the Treasury and hand it to a new No 10 department in Manchester. The DEA was responsible for drawing up a national plan for the economy, which began with the timeless exhortation: “We must pay our way in the world and produce more wealth inside this country.” The baleful influence of the Treasury, with its stranglehold over the public finances, has long been lamented by leftwingers, who accuse it of short-term thinking and ingrained, institutional caution. “The dual job of growth and control of the public finances sometimes clouds the growth mission,” Burnham told the Times. “Having No 10 leading on that growth mission means you’ve got maximum power to unlock the blockages where they exist in the Whitehall system.” Some of the most criticised decisions of Keir Starmer’s tenure were seen by many Labour MPs as resulting from this “Treasury brain” – from slashing winter fuel allowance to caving in to City lobbying on a bank windfall tax. Burnham hopes the new prime minister’s department, overseen by his powerful cabinet ally Louise Haigh, will open the space for some fresh thinking. “The new No 10 North innovation is more significant than people realise,” he said. Burnham’s route to growth runs through devolution One of the few detailed policy publications the new cabinet has so far produced was on radical plans for devolution. The PM hopes handing additional powers to metro mayors will help bring together growth policies now scattered across Whitehall. Ruth Curtice, director of the Resolution Foundation thinktank and a former longtime Treasury official, says coordinating across these different policy areas – housing, education, planning and so on – could be the most effective use of the new Manchester-based unit. “No one department has all of the levers – the Treasury don’t own all of the levers,” she says. “I would see it as a positive thing that this No 10 says, ‘Given what a priority this is, we’re going to put more force behind it.’” Former Brown adviser Michael Jacobs, emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield, draws a comparison with the Office for Climate Change, which helped to coordinate policy across government. “The really interesting version of this to me would be a new growth unit, drawing on and made up of officials from all the relevant departments.” Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, points out that Burnham’s pick for chancellor, John Healey, was instrumental in the creation of regional development agencies, way back in the Blair-Brown era. These were meant to bring a regional dimension to growth and industrial policy – but were scrapped by the 2010 Conservative-Lib Dem coalition. George Osborne went on to create and empower city region mayors as the focus for devolution. Given the pair’s joint interest in devolution, Raja argues that far from clipping Healey’s wings, “this is one of the more merged tag teams in No 10 and No 11 that we have seen”. Treasury power is inescapable Yet not everyone is convinced that it makes sense to create a policy counterweight to the Treasury. Former Conservative chief secretary to the Treasury David Gauke says the Treasury’s control over tax and spend, which it will maintain under the shake-up, means it is inevitably powerful. “The Treasury is always going to be the most important department.” Indeed, he suspects stripping growth out of the Treasury’s remit would just exaggerate its tendency to fixate on penny-pinching. He also questions whether No 10 North can work: “You’re going to have this office, which will get at best a day a week of face-time with the PM, and little access to other ministers – and it will be trying to push the government in a more pro-growth direction.” A Treasury source stresses that, as the initial government announcement said, No 10 North will focus on “local growth”, and in particular devolution – rather than taking over economic strategy from No 11. The Treasury has “lent” a small number of staff to the new unit, while its second permanent secretary, Beth Russell, who was instrumental in the creation of the Treasury’s own northern outpost, the Darlington Economic Campus, has been working closely with the Manchester team. More civil servants are being transferred from other departments, including housing and local government, and former Times journalist Sam Lister has been appointed as No 10 North’s director. However, Whitehall veterans point to the new department’s relatively modest resources thus far. Jonathan Portes, a former senior government economist and now professor at King’s College London, says the most important question, as Burnham’s new arrangements bed in, will be how the inevitable policy clashes will be resolved. “What happens when No 10 wants to do something, and Treasury says no – or says, ‘yes, we’ll pay lip service to this but don’t expect any spending to go along with it’?” he says. “That has been the historic response of the Treasury when No 10 has got more powerful.” Hannah Peaker, deputy chief executive of the New Economics Foundation thinktank, says the priority should be ensuring economic decision-makers – including the Treasury and No 10, but also the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility – work better together. “While a more devolved approach could help accelerate regional growth, the most important remedy is better coordination between economic institutions so that they are all pulling in the same direction.” Will No 10 North open the space for more radicalism? In an article for the progressive Renewal journal earlier this year, Haigh complained of the Treasury that, “faced with the dual mandate of maintaining fiscal control and supporting economic growth, the institution defaults toward caution, prioritising near-term debt dynamics over longer-term economic outcomes”. In the run-up to Burnham’s bid for power, he appeared to suggest large-scale renationalisation of public utilities and radical tax reform would be on his agenda – alongside the long-promised shake-up of social care. But some of these ambitious and potentially costly plans are likely to come into sharp conflict with the institutional caution Haigh identified. With a critical budget fast approaching, the new cabinet – north and south – faces a string of decisions on tax and spend; and other key choices loom, including on how to shape the future of the beleaguered privatised water industry. In the run-up to the last two Labour budgets, debate was dominated by the immediate challenges for fiscal policy, often played out noisily in public against a backdrop of febrile government bond markets. Burnham clearly hopes to shape a different debate, both inside and outside government, but the historic precedent he highlighted, in the Wilson era, underlines the difficulties of reining in the Treasury. Wilson’s temperamental secretary of state for economic affairs, George Brown, moved on after two years, by which time the national plan had been blown way off course. His role was then downgraded so it was no longer a cabinet position and, by 1969, the experiment with a separate Department for Economic Affairs was over – and its powers had been sucked back into the Treasury.

Title: England v Pakistan: first men’s cricket Test, day one – as it happened
Content: And I think that’s enough from me, especially as I can’t see any pictures. Thanks for sticking with us during the blackout – Ali’s report will land here soon and we’ll be back tomorrow for day two. Bye! And how about the hat-trick ball? “I didn’t like the break as I was on a roll, but we were happy we got the last few wickets.” Josh Tongue:“It was quite nice to bowl on. You had to be brave with your lengths, but got your rewards by targeting your stumps as much as you can and that’s how I got my wickets.” Who has the match ball? “Robbo had to start with but the groundsman has now split it in half. “ “This Mo Ali floats it like a beach ball and stings the batters like a kitten.” Thank you Abishek Chopra! And sorry about that last half hour, I’m not sure what technical hiccup there was there. An excellent day for England, especially Robinson and Tongue who finished with five wickets each. And a bit of a miserable one for Pakistan, who look a good seamer short of a full attack. 25th over: England 112-2 (Cox 23, Root 37) Root takes a single from the penultimate ball of the day and Cox leaves the last to complete an almost pitch-perfect performance. 24th over: England 111-2 (Cox 23, Root 36) Does a Joe Root hundred feel inevitable? Yes it does. He tucks into a short one from Ali and sends another through. mid off. 23rd over: England 103-2 (Cox 22, Root 29) It sounds very beery in Leeds. Root brings up England’s hundred, they’re galloping up on Pakistan. “Tanya, if you lose the pictures, are we supposed to send you the obo commentary? It’s the least we can do really. “Yes, Abishek Chopra, please do, poste haste.” 22nd over: England 98-2 (Cox 21, Root 25) Hosing it down in Manchester, not sure if it is blowing east. Root brings up the fifty partnership with a Rootish clip for four off Khurram. 21st over: England 94-2 (Cox 21, Root 21) Three from Ali’s over. Can I just ask what channel people are watching the cricket on, mine all seem to have cut off… 19th over: England 90-2 (Cox 21, Root 17) A back foot punch brings Cox four from Abbas, but no more runs from the over. I’’m having a few technical problems here a sec, seem to have lost the pictures. 17th over: England 86-2 (Cox 17, Root 17) Khurram replaces Ali and immediately donates Root a ball short and wide outside off stump, which Root could cut for four with his eyes shut - and duly does. Khurra m over compensates next ball, and four leg byes follow. A third four, as Root posts through square leg, though Abbas could have shown a little bit more enthusiasm for chasing it down. 16th over: England 74-2 (Cox 17, Root 9) A ninth almost immaculate over for Abbas. At slip, and wearing a huge cable knit with PEPSI across the front, Salman Ali Agha considers his options. 16th over: England 72-2 (Cox 15, Root 9) Root is in watchful mood. As Ali runs through his over, we learn that he has a BA in English literature as his parents said he could only play cricket if he continued his education. Five dots then a short ball which Root duly dispatches through the covers for four. 15th over: England 68-2 (Cox 15, Root 5) The Barmy Army are finding their evening voice. A lovely over from Abbas. Hello Oli Booth. “I too never saw Wes Hall live, but in my younger years I spoke to plenty of old timers who’d faced him in the northern league. He was absolutely, terrifyingly magnificent and, by all accounts, an even better man too.” 14th over: England 67-2 (Cox 15, Root 4) Ali is mixing dross with diamonds – Cox squirms at one that nips away between slip and gully for four but then fires the next through the covers with gumption for four more. 13th over: England 55-2 (Cox 6, Root 1) Rizwan is up to the stumps, Abbas shimmies in, his ears illuminated by the Leeds evening sun. Root has his work cut out in this over, Abbas weaving magic, the penultimate ball jagging back in off the seam leaving Root all at sea. Mark Butcher is discussing Gay’s dismissal. “What you want not to do as a left hander is cross your right foot over your left one, your shoulders then follow and you end up chest on. It’s a common nightmare for left handers and its something I would train very hard to do to make sure my feet weren’t beyond parallel.” 12th over: England 55-2 (Cox 6, Root 1) Ali, long run up, arms flailing like a 5000m runner as he reaches the stumps. Just one from the over as they take the final drinks break of the day. 11th over: England 54-2 (Cox 6, Root 0) Abbas’ sixth over. Cox gets off the mark by flaying a friendly wide ball for four through the covers. Mohammad Ali is the first change. Gay purrs three fours in the over, but Ali gets his man with the final delivery as Gay is suddenly wooden, turned around, legs twisted, and edges to second slip. 10th over: England 48-2 (Cox 0, Root 0) 9th over: England 36-1 (Gay 21, Cox 0) Duckett is beaten by one that zips away off the seam, and loses his wicket next ball to one that straightens all the way home. “So happy to see Gay open in place of Crawley,” writes Michael Inglis. “These glorious off drives and clear leaves...” I actually enjoyed watching Crawley too, but there certainly feels less jeopardy with Gay. And his strokes are sublime. Clonked on the front pad just above the ankle. Given out on the field, Duckett screws up his face and asks Gay what he thinks. Tricky to send a senior partner on his way and they review, to no avail. 8th over: England 36-0 (Duckett 15, Gay 17) Another Crackerjack four from Gay, this time a square drive, is followed by five dots from Khurram’s fourth over. 7th over: England 32-0 (Duckett 15, Gay 17) Abbas snakes one past the outside edge of Gay’s bat as he leans forwards. But he picks up three next ball. Duckett picks up another couple through the covers – he’s moving along nicely though is yet to score a boundary. “What about Wesley Hall? Where does he rank amongst the choices?” asks Michael Coad. Ah Michael, I think this conversation links back to Rob’s stint earlier this afternoon. I never watched Hall in the flesh, though he was terrifying by all accounts, but I am old enough to have seen Garner, Holding and Marshall and they were all magnificent. 6th over: England 27-0 (Duckett 7, Gay 14) The wished-for wicket not coming here for Pakistan. Come Headingley clouds. Hello David Harris! “Lovely to see you on a Test OBO, but can we trust you’ll be back guiding us through the CC from tomorrow?” [I will be in Derby, on Stokes watch, should the rain fall and any OBO readers be bored] “Anyway, in over 47 you said you couldn’t recall another season where rain had been so wished for - I can certainly remember matches where the subject line applied, in fact, I think some bunch of chancers even put out a book with that title.” Very good, and thank you. 5th over: England 21-0 (Duckett 7, Gay 14) Abbas again, snake hipped, gazelle lean. Gay clips a fuller ball to the rope, and follows up with a silver service cover drive. A neat defensive shot from a lofty height – he must be six foot something – full stops the over. 4th over: England 13-0 (Duckett 6, Gay 7) The umpire raises a quarter of an eyebrow about Khurram’s follow through and the over ends with a Duckett leave. 3rd over: England 11-0 (Duckett 6, Gay 5) Nice to remember Pep Guardiola being turned down for the plush suite in the Aegeas Bowl Hilton as it was “reserved for Mohammad”, as Abbas tests Gay for five balls – before Gay gloriously drives a half-volley to the cover boundary. 2nd over: England 7-0 (Duckett 6, Gay 1) Khurram from the Kirkstall lane end. Gay, on a pair after the warm-up game, escapes the pressure with a single. In the shade of the dressing room, Harry Brook drinks a carton of something that looks like a milkshake. 1st over: England 4-0 (Duckett 4, Gay 0) Jerusalem is still being belted out as Pakistan review an lbw decision against Duckett’s back leg. Ooof, unlucky, it’s good but umpire’s call on height. Abbas proving a predictable menace in these conditions. The roller rolls. Rizwan throws the ball from glove to glove. Mohammad Abbas is straight-faced in mirrored shades. “Afternoon.” Hello Tom van der Gucht. “Robinson seems almost more threatening and successful in Tests than county games which seems almost counter intuitive as it’s meant to be a step up... “Is it because he’s being backed-up by more potent change bowlers than when playing for Sussex? Is it because international players from other countries have less experience of the conditions? Is he a big match player who takes it up a notch in front of large crowds?
